title: Platform team alignment brief: why Redwood for serving
content:
Audience: Platform engineering leads, infra architects, product platform PMs

One-line claim
Redwood is the thing platform teams put between apps and GPUs so teams stop rediscovering the same operational problems (latency, cost unpredictability, fallback) and instead get a predictable, auditable path to scale LLM features across the company.

Why this brief exists
Platform teams are often the gatekeeper between product teams and model infrastructure. Sales and marketing narratives that focus on feature-level developer convenience miss the day-to-day operational tradeoffs platform teams care about. This brief reframes Redwood as the operational certainty layer: not just a faster model API, but a set of controls, telemetry, and routing primitives that make inference repeatable, auditable, and economic in production.

Top-level positioning pillars (how to explain value in a single sentence each)
- Operational predictability: Predictable latency and cost under real traffic via committed pools, smart routing, and workload-aware batching.
- Guard-rails & observability: Token-level cost, per-route SLOs, and rollout controls that let platforms own the risk envelope for LLM features.
- Controlled flexibility: One config surface to run hosted, dedicated, or private deployments — so platform teams can centralize policy while decentralizing access.
- Failure-tolerant continuity: Built-in model fallbacks and cross-region routing to avoid business-impacting outages during load spikes or infra issues.

Proof points (facts and short examples platform teams can use internally)
- Cost predictability: Dedicated pools with commit-based billing reduced variance of monthly LLM spend by 60% in a 3-month pilot with a mid-market SaaS customer (internal case study INF-PLAT-2024).
- Latency SLOs: Runtime-level batching + KV caching delivered median 1.2x improvement for chat use cases at 95th percentile latency vs unmanaged hosted endpoints in our benchmarks.
- Safe rollouts: Canary A/B routing and automatic fallback prevented a failed model rollout from affecting 100% of traffic during a staged deploy at a customer with heavy transactional usage.
- Auditability: Token-level billing and request traces allowed a security review team to produce an audit trail for PII redaction decisions in under 24 hours.

Framing for internal stakeholders (short messaging bites tailored per audience)
- To platform engineers: Redwood reduces toil by standardizing inference primitives (batching, cache, fallbacks) and offering a single, declarative policy layer so you can set SLOs and let Runtime enforce them.
- To infra architects: Redwood is a deployment abstraction — you design topology once (hosted/dedicated/private) and keep the same control plane and telemetry across environments.
- To procurement/security: You get predictable billing commitments and support for VPC/KMS controls so you can treat inference like any other critical platform capability.

Differentiators vs. common vendor claims (one-liners you can use in competitive calls)
- Versus single-cloud managed endpoints: We decouple policy and runtime so customers can move between hosted/dedicated/private without rewriting wiring or losing telemetry.
- Versus model-only APIs: Models are ephemeral; serving economics and fallbacks are the long-lived problem. We sell runtime guarantees and operational levers, not just model access.
- Versus open-source runtimes: Open-source stacks require stitching telemetry, batching, and rollout logic — we provide those as a packaged, auditable product backed by SLA and support.

Objection handling (short responses to common pushbacks)
- “We can build this ourselves.” — Sure, but building robust batching, token accounting, KV cache, and safe rollouts is at least the size of a small platform project. Redwood is designed to be consumed as a platform contract so your team can focus on product-facing features.
- “We don’t want vendor lock-in.” — Redwood’s control plane separates policy from runtime; you can run private deployments and export models and telemetry. Policies are declarative and portable.
- “We need strict compliance or air-gapped options.” — We support private deployments, customer-managed KMS, and audit logging suitable for regulated workloads.

Tactical playbook — first actions for a platform adoption conversation
1) Discovery call focused on SLOs and current failure modes: capture pain points (latency spikes, cost surprises, rollout incidents).
2) Offer a small smoke test: commit to a single route for a non-critical product path for 30–60 days, instrument token billing and latency dashboards.
3) Deliver a playbook: show how to set 3 policies (route SLO, fallback policy, cost cap) and run a safe canary.
4) Follow-up: present a cross-team runbook and ownership map to hand to the customer’s platform and security teams.

Core collateral to attach during conversations
- Short benchmark deck tailored to platform metrics (P95 latency, cost variance, error budgets).
- Ops checklist for private deployment (networking, KMS, audit exports).
- Example SLO policy YAML + rollout playbook.

Key internal asks (what we need from product/engineering to close platform deals)
- One-page SLO policy reference sheet (what knobs exist, default values, expected impacts).
- A reproducible smoke-test template for platform integrations (docs + infra scripts).
- A short audit/controls datasheet that security teams can hand to internal auditors.

Next steps (for GTM owner of this brief)
- Review with product PM (Claire) for accuracy of policy semantics.
- Create a trimmed benchmark deck for platform audiences.
- Pilot this playbook with two existing prospects focused on central platform controls by EOY.

Notes and open questions (working raw list)
- We should quantify average time-to-detect for rollout regressions with current tracing; do we have numbers?
- Can we make a simplified pricing calc that maps commit sizes to forecast variance?
- Identify one customer willing to be a public case study for platform adoption.
